items.topic: Cane fitting — handle at wrist crease; elbow slightly bent
items.stem: The nurse fits a single-point cane for a client with left-leg weakness. Which fitting instruction is correct?

options.text: With the client standing upright, the cane handle should be at the crease of the wrist and the elbow slightly bent when holding the handle
Set the handle at shoulder height so the elbow is locked straight
Set the handle below the knee so the client must lean far forward
Ignore height and teach the client to hold the cane on the same side as the weak leg

rationales.A: Correct. MedlinePlus: handle at wrist level; elbow slightly bent. AAOS: top of cane reaches wrist crease; elbow slightly bent.
rationales.B: Incorrect. A locked straight elbow at shoulder height is too high and reduces control.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Too-low setting forces unsafe forward lean.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Height must be adjusted; cane is held opposite the weak/injured side (already taught separately).

items.topic: NGN matrix — safe cane use teaching indicated vs not
items.stem: For safe use of a single-point cane after unilateral lower-extremity injury, indicate whether each teaching point is Indicated or Not indicated.

rows.text: Adjust the handle to the crease of the wrist with the elbow slightly bent
Hold the cane in the hand opposite the injured/weaker leg
Place weight on the cane before the tip (or all prongs) is on the ground
Look forward while walking rather than continuously down at the feet

rationales.R1: Indicated. MedlinePlus/AAOS: wrist-crease height; slight elbow bend.
rationales.R2: Indicated. MedlinePlus/AAOS: hold cane opposite weak/injured side.
rationales.R3: Not indicated. MedlinePlus: tip or all prongs on ground before putting weight on cane.
rationales.R4: Indicated. MedlinePlus: look forward, not down at feet.

items.topic: Cane on stairs — up with stronger leg first; down with weaker/injured leg first
items.stem: The nurse teaches stair safety with a cane after right ankle surgery. Which instruction is correct?

options.text: Going up, step up with the stronger (uninjured) leg first; going down, lead with the cane and the weaker/injured leg, then the stronger leg
Always lead with the injured leg when going up and down
Carry the cane and hop on the injured leg without using a handrail when available
Place both feet on each step before moving the cane, ignoring which leg is stronger

rationales.A: Correct. MedlinePlus: up — stronger leg first, then cane and weaker leg; down — cane then weaker then stronger. AAOS: up on good leg first; down cane then injured then good leg.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Leading with the injured leg when ascending is unsafe.
rationales.C: Incorrect. AAOS: use free hand on handrail when available; do not hop on injured leg.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Sequence depends on stronger vs weaker leg for ascent and descent.

items.topic: NGN cloze — cane stair sequence up with good / down with bad
items.stem: Complete the teaching for stair safety with a cane after unilateral lower-extremity injury.

ngn.template: When going up stairs, step up first with the {B1} leg. When going down, place the cane on the lower step, then step down with the {B2} leg before the stronger leg.

rationales.B1a: Incorrect. Ascending leads with the stronger/uninjured leg.
rationales.B1b: Correct. MedlinePlus/AAOS: go up with stronger/good leg first.
rationales.B1c: Incorrect. Sequence is specific, not random.
rationales.B2a: Incorrect. Descending leads with cane and weaker/injured leg.
rationales.B2b: Correct. MedlinePlus/AAOS: down with cane then weaker/injured leg, then stronger.
rationales.B2c: Incorrect. Legs move in sequenced steps, not as a simultaneous hop.

items.topic: Heating pad safety — do not fall asleep with pad in place
items.stem: The nurse teaches a client home use of an electric heating pad for muscle spasm pain. Which instruction is the priority safety teaching?

options.text: Do not fall asleep with the heating pad in place
Sleep all night with the pad on the highest setting
Place the bare heating element directly on open broken skin
Ignore redness or blistering because warmth always means healing

rationales.A: Correct. MedlinePlus: to prevent skin injury, do not fall asleep with a heating pad in place. Mayo Clinic: never sleep with a heating pad.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Overnight high-heat use increases burn risk.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Heat on open/broken skin is contraindicated in heat-safety teaching.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Redness/blistering signals overheating/burn risk and requires stopping heat.

items.topic: Blood/body-fluid spill — PPE, remove visible soil, then disinfect; hand hygiene after
items.client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
items.stem: A small amount of blood spills on a hard floor in a client care area. Which nursing action is correct?

options.text: Don gloves (add gown/face protection if splash risk), wipe up the blood, apply facility-approved disinfectant, then remove PPE and perform hand hygiene
Wipe the spill with bare hands and leave the area wet without disinfectant
Spray disinfectant into the air over the spill without wearing gloves
Ignore small blood spills because housekeeping surfaces never transmit bloodborne pathogens

rationales.A: Correct. CDC: PPE, remove visible blood, then disinfect. PHO home/community IPAC: gloves (± gown/face protection), wipe up blood, apply disinfectant, remove PPE and hand hygiene.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Bare-hand contact and omitting disinfection are unsafe.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Gloves are required; aerosolizing disinfectant over a spill is not the recommended process.
rationales.D: Incorrect. CDC still requires prompt cleaning and disinfection of blood spills.

items.topic: N95/FFR — perform user seal check each donning; not a substitute for fit testing
items.client_needs_subcategory: Safety and Infection Prevention and Control
items.stem: Before entering an Airborne Precautions room, the nurse dons a fit-tested N95 respirator. Which action is required?

options.text: Perform a user seal check each time the respirator is put on; a seal check does not replace fit testing
Skip the seal check because last year's fit test permanently guarantees today's seal
Treat a quick seal check as a full substitute for never having been fit tested
Wear the respirator loosely under the chin without checking for leaks

rationales.A: Correct. NIOSH: seal check every time respirator is donned; not a substitute for fit testing. OSHA: employees perform a user seal check each time they put on a tight-fitting respirator.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Fit testing selects model/size; seal must still be checked with each donning.
rationales.C: Incorrect. NIOSH explicitly states seal check is not a substitute for fit testing.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Tight face seal is required for FFR protection.

items.topic: Therapeutic communication — prefer open-ended invitation; avoid accusatory why questions
items.stem: A client says, "I feel like everything is falling apart." Which nurse response best uses therapeutic communication?

options.text: "Tell me more about what has been going on for you."
"Why did you let things get this bad?"
"At least you are not as sick as some other people here."
"You should just stop worrying and think positive."

rationales.A: Correct. OpenStax Fundamentals: open-ended questions support therapeutic communication. OpenStax PMH: explore with open-ended questions rather than accusatory why or minimizing remarks.
rationales.B: Incorrect. OpenStax PMH: asking why can imply accusation/judgment and provoke defensiveness.
rationales.C: Incorrect. Minimizing remarks belittle the client's feelings.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Advice-giving/false positivity is nontherapeutic compared with open exploration.

items.topic: NGN bowtie — acute situational anxiety: recognize; therapeutic presence/open-ended; monitor distress
items.stem: After unexpected bad news, a client paces, reports a racing heart, and says, "I can't think straight." Complete the bowtie: the priority condition, two priority actions, and two parameters to monitor.

actions.text: Stay with the client and invite discussion with an open-ended prompt
Leave immediately so the client can 'tough it out' alone
Use calm presence; allow brief silence and avoid minimizing remarks
Demand, "Why are you overreacting like this?"
Tell the client their problem is trivial compared with terminal illness

parameters.text: Self-reported distress and ability to communicate needs
Breathing pattern, heart rate trend, and safety behaviours

rationales.K1: Correct. Merck: anxiety involves fear/anxiety with behavioural changes; cue pattern fits acute distress after a stressor.
rationales.K3: Incorrect. No opioid toxicity pattern (e.g., pinpoint pupils, apnea).
rationales.K4: Incorrect. Vertigo alone does not explain pacing and catastrophic thinking after bad news.
rationales.A1: Correct. OpenStax: open-ended prompts and offering self/presence support therapeutic communication.
rationales.A2: Incorrect. Leaving a highly distressed client alone is not supportive acute care.
rationales.A3: Correct. OpenStax: silence and avoiding minimizing support processing.
rationales.A4: Incorrect. Accusatory why questions are nontherapeutic.
rationales.P1: Correct. Monitor whether distress eases and communication remains coherent.
rationales.P2: Correct. Anxiety has somatic/arousal features; monitor breathing, HR trend, and safety.

items.jurisdiction_note: CNO Code/Social Media guidance + PHIPA: do not disclose client personal health information (including identifiable images/stories) on social media without proper authority/consent; de-identification must make identification unreasonable.
items.topic: Ontario — do not post client PHI/images on social media (CNO / PHIPA)
items.stem: An Ontario RN considers posting a selfie from the unit that clearly shows a client's face and unique wound dressing in the background, with the caption "Tough day in wound care." Which action meets privacy accountabilities?

options.text: Do not post the photo or any identifiable client health information on social media
Post it because the client's name is not written in the caption
Post it on a private account because private platforms never create privacy risk
Post it first and ask the client for consent afterwards

rationales.A: Correct. CNO: do not share client information/images on social media; health-record content including unique findings is inappropriate to post. PHIPA guidance: never disclose PHI on social media without unpressured consent; be prudent not to post workplace pictures that may include clients.
rationales.B: Incorrect. Omitting a name does not prevent identification from a face/unique clinical image.
rationales.C: Incorrect. CNO cautions against sharing even on private platforms because content may still be identifiable/shared.
rationales.D: Incorrect. Consent must be obtained before disclosure; posting first violates privacy.

sources.title: Social Media: Reflect before you post
sources.section: Confidentiality and Privacy – Personal Health Information
sources.evidence: Do not share client information/images on social media; even de-identified posts may identify clients.
